items.title: Digital Root Test
items.question: A five-digit number uses each of the digits 2, 4, 5, 7, and 8 exactly once. Without seeing the number, what remainder must it leave when divided by 3?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. The digit sum is 26, and 26 leaves remainder 2 modulo 3, so every arrangement does too.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. Add the digits to get 26, and 26 divided by 3 leaves 2. Divisibility by 3 depends only on the digit sum, never on their order.
items.lessonContent:
Divisibility by 3 lives in the digit sum, not the digit order.
Adding digits first collapses huge arrangements into one small check.
Remainders transfer from the sum to the whole number.
Invariants beat brute force whenever order is irrelevant.
Share this: test tonight whether a shuffled phone number keeps its remainder mod 3.

items.title: Nines Check
items.question: A number's digits add up to 41. What remainder does that number leave when divided by 9?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Since 41 divided by 9 leaves 5, the original number must leave the same remainder.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 5. Reduce the digit sum 41 modulo 9 to get 5. A number always shares its remainder mod 9 with its digit sum.
items.lessonContent:
Casting out nines turns giant numbers into single-digit checks.
Digit sums preserve remainders modulo 9.
Repeat the reduction until one small number remains.
Ancient accountants used this to catch multiplication errors.
Share this: verify one receipt total tonight using digit sums.

items.title: Eleven Balance
items.question: For a certain ticket number, the alternating sum of its digits (first minus second plus third, and so on) equals 22. What remainder does the ticket number leave when divided by 11?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. A multiple of 11 in the alternating sum means the number itself is a multiple of 11.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 0. Since 22 is twice 11, the alternating-sum test declares the number divisible by 11. The alternating sum and the number share their remainder mod 11.
items.lessonContent:
Divisibility by 11 hides in alternating plus-minus digit sums.
A multiple in the test value certifies the whole number.
Positional weights of plus and minus one do the silent work.
One clever checksum replaces pages of long division.
Share this: test your own ticket stub for divisibility by 11.

items.title: Power Last Digit
items.question: The powers of 7 end in repeating last digits 7, 9, 3, 1. Following that cycle, what is the last digit of 7 raised to the 100th power?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Since 100 is a multiple of the cycle length 4, the pattern lands back on 1.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 1. Divide the exponent 100 by the cycle length 4: the remainder 0 means the cycle completes fully and ends on 1.
items.lessonContent:
Last digits of powers always fall into short cycles.
Find the cycle length once, then reduce the exponent.
Only the remainder of exponent divided by cycle length matters.
Huge powers shrink to tiny clock arithmetic.
Share this: predict the last digit of 3 to the 50th tonight.

items.title: Common Multiples Count
items.question: How many integers from 1 to 100 are divisible by both 3 and 4?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Being divisible by both 3 and 4 means divisible by 12, and 100 holds 8 multiples of 12.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 8. Combine the conditions using their least common multiple 12, then count multiples of 12 up to 100: 12, 24, up to 96.
items.lessonContent:
Combined divisibility conditions merge through least common multiples.
Counting multiples is division rounded down.
Two conditions become one cleaner condition.
List endpoints to confirm the count never drifts by one.
Share this: count tonight how many bus numbers under 50 are multiples of 6.

items.title: Coprime Census
items.question: How many integers from 1 to 30 share no common factor with 30 other than 1?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Removing multiples of 2, 3, and 5 from 1 to 30 leaves exactly 8 survivors.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 8. Strike out everything sharing 2, 3, or 5 with 30; the remaining 1, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, and 29 are the coprime set.
items.lessonContent:
Coprimality means sharing no prime factor at all.
Listing by elimination beats testing pairs one by one.
Prime factors of the modulus decide every exclusion.
Counting survivors previews Euler's totient idea.
Share this: find tonight which numbers under 12 are coprime to 12.

items.title: Twin Remainders
items.question: A positive integer leaves remainder 2 when divided by 3 and remainder 3 when divided by 5. What is the smallest such integer?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Listing numbers that are 3 mod 5 gives 3, 8, 13, and 8 is the first that is also 2 mod 3.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 8. Candidates leaving remainder 3 mod 5 are 3, 8, 13, and so on; checking each mod 3 shows 8 is the first fit.
items.lessonContent:
Simultaneous remainders yield to listing one progression.
Generate candidates from the larger modulus to finish faster.
Test each candidate against the second condition in turn.
First fit is minimal by construction of the ordered list.
Share this: solve tonight which locker numbers satisfy two remainder clues.

items.title: Million Mod Seven
items.question: What remainder does ten to the sixth power leave when divided by 7?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Since 10 behaves like 3 mod 7 and 3 to the sixth is 729, which is one more than a multiple of 7.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 1. Replace 10 with its remainder 3, raise to the sixth to get 729, and 729 divided by 7 leaves 1.
items.lessonContent:
Huge powers shrink when reduced before multiplying.
Replace each base by its small remainder first.
Remainders multiply just like the original numbers.
One simplification early saves pages of arithmetic later.
Share this: reduce 100 mod 7 tonight before anyone reaches for a calculator.

items.title: Triangular Remainder
items.question: The sum of the integers from 1 to 100 equals 5050. What remainder does that sum leave when divided by 7?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Subtracting the largest multiple of 7 below 5050 leaves 3.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. Since 7 times 721 is 5047, the sum 5050 exceeds it by 3. Only the excess over a full multiple survives as remainder.
items.lessonContent:
Remainders of big totals need only nearby multiples.
Find the closest clean multiple below the target.
The gap between total and multiple is the answer.
Estimate first, then verify the multiple exactly.
Share this: check tonight what 1000 leaves mod 7 without dividing fully.

items.title: Divisor Census
items.question: Including 1 and itself, how many positive divisors does 72 have?
items.correctExplanation: Right. From 72 equals 2 cubed times 3 squared, the count is 4 times 3, which is 12.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 12. Factor 72 into 2 cubed times 3 squared, add one to each exponent, and multiply: 4 times 3 gives 12 divisors.
items.lessonContent:
Prime exponents encode the whole divisor structure.
Adding one per exponent counts every combination choice.
Factoring once answers infinitely many divisor questions.
Multiplication of independent choices is the counting engine.
Share this: count the divisors of 60 tonight from its prime factors.

items.title: Rope Pieces
items.question: Two ropes measure 48 metres and 60 metres. Both must be cut into equal-length pieces as long as possible with nothing left over. How long is each piece in metres?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. The greatest common divisor of 48 and 60 is 12, so 12-metre pieces fit both perfectly.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 12. List common divisors of 48 and 60 and take the largest: 12 divides both with nothing left, and nothing longer does.
items.lessonContent:
Greatest common divisors solve fairest-split problems.
Shared measures must divide every given length.
Largest feasible beats merely feasible for longest pieces.
Euclid's algorithm finds it without listing everything.
Share this: split two snack bars evenly tonight using common divisors.

items.title: Blinking Sync
items.question: Two signal lights blink every 6 seconds and every 8 seconds. Starting together, after how many seconds do they next blink at the same moment?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The least common multiple of 6 and 8 is 24, the first shared blink after the start.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 24. Multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, and multiples of 8 are 8, 16, 24: the first meeting point is 24 seconds.
items.lessonContent:
Repeating schedules meet at common multiples.
The least one is the first reunion after the start.
Listing multiples reveals the meeting visibly.
Prime factors build it faster for large periods.
Share this: predict tonight when two microwave timers beep together.

items.title: Eighth Append
items.question: The digits 7, 1, 4 are followed by one unknown digit to form a four-digit multiple of 8. What is the smallest digit that works?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Since 7140 leaves remainder 4 mod 8, appending 4 completes the next full multiple, 7144.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 4. Compute 7140 mod 8 to get 4, so the final digit must supply the missing 4. Trying digits upward from 0 confirms 4 is the first success.
items.lessonContent:
Appending a digit adds a small adjustable remainder.
Measure the shortfall of the stem first.
The missing digit must exactly fill that gap.
Trying digits in order guarantees the smallest answer.
Share this: test tonight which final digit makes your house number divisible by 8.

items.title: Product Checksum
items.question: A student claims 123 times 456 equals 56082. The digit-sum check says the product mod 9 should be 0. What is 56082 mod 9, exposing the error?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The digits of 56082 sum to 21, then to 3, so it cannot be the true product.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. Add the claimed product's digits to get 21 and reduce again to 3. Since the true product must reduce to 0 mod 9, the claim fails the checksum.
items.lessonContent:
Checksums catch errors without recomputing everything.
Digit sums must agree on both sides of a multiplication.
One mismatch proves a mistake even before the fix appears.
Verification is cheaper than recalculation at scale.
Share this: checksum one multiplication tonight before trusting the display.

items.title: Quarter Hundred Count
items.question: How many positive multiples of 25 lie strictly below 300?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. The multiples run 25, 50, up to 275, which is 11 of them.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 11. Divide 300 by 25 to get 12, then exclude 300 itself since the bound is strict. The list ends at 275.
items.lessonContent:
Strict bounds exclude the endpoint itself.
Division counts multiples including the boundary.
Subtracting the endpoint case fixes off-by-one slips.
State whether below means strict before counting.
Share this: count tonight how many 50s fit strictly below 500.

items.title: Fourth Power Clock
items.question: What remainder does three to the fourth power leave upon division by 8?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Since three to the fourth is 81, and 81 minus 80 (ten eights) leaves 1.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 1. Compute 3 to the fourth as 81, then subtract 10 lots of 8 to reach 80. The leftover 1 is the remainder.
items.lessonContent:
Landmark powers reward memorization plus adjustment.
Compare the power with nearby clean multiples.
The small excess over a multiple is the remainder.
1024 sits one above a multiple of both 11 and 3.
Share this: find tonight what 2 to the eighth leaves mod 11.

items.title: Repunit Triple
items.question: What is the smallest positive multiple of 3 whose decimal digits are all ones?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Single 1 fails and 11 fails, but 111 has digit sum 3 and divides cleanly by 3.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 111. Test repunits in order: 1 and 11 are not multiples of 3, while 111 with digit sum 3 succeeds first.
items.lessonContent:
Digit-sum tests turn existence hunts into short lists.
Test candidates in increasing order for minimality.
Each extra one adds exactly one to the digit sum.
Structure plus ordering proves smallest, not just valid.
Share this: hunt tonight for the smallest all-ones multiple of 9.

items.title: Triple Product Rule
items.question: The product of any three consecutive positive integers is always divisible by which single-digit number larger than 5?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Among any three consecutive integers one is even and one is a multiple of 3, forcing divisibility by 6.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 6. Every run of three consecutive numbers contains a multiple of 2 and a multiple of 3, and 2 times 3 guarantees a factor of 6.
items.lessonContent:
Consecutive runs guarantee small factors by pigeonhole logic.
One even plus one multiple-of-three forces a factor six.
Divisibility can be certain without knowing the numbers.
Density arguments replace case-by-case checking.
Share this: test tonight that five consecutive numbers always hide a multiple of 5.

items.title: Square Mod Four
items.question: A perfect square divided by 4 can leave remainder 0 or which other remainder?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Even squares are 0 mod 4 while odd squares are always 1 mod 4, with nothing else possible.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 1. Write an odd number as 2k plus 1 and square it: the result is 4 times something plus 1. No square ever leaves 2 or 3 mod 4.
items.lessonContent:
Squares occupy surprisingly few remainder classes.
Parity decides the square's behavior mod 4.
Algebra on 2k and 2k plus 1 settles every case.
Impossible remainders are powerful proof tools.
Share this: show tonight that no square ends in remainder 2 mod 4.

items.title: Cube Mod Nine
items.question: What remainder does five cubed leave when divided by 9?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Since 5 cubed is 125, and 125 minus 117 (thirteen nines) leaves 8.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 8. Compute 5 cubed as 125, then subtract 13 lots of 9 to reach 117. The leftover 8 is the remainder.
items.lessonContent:
Small cubes stay checkable by hand.
Compute the power, then strip full multiples.
Nearby multiples give the remainder directly.
Manual remainders keep modular intuition honest.
Share this: find tonight what 4 cubed leaves mod 9.

items.title: Sixes Range
items.question: How many two-digit numbers are divisible by 6?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. They run from 12 to 96 in steps of 6, which is 15 numbers.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 15. Start at the first two-digit multiple 12 and end at 96; the count is 96 minus 12 over 6 plus one.
items.lessonContent:
Counting multiples in a range uses endpoints.
Subtract, divide by step, then add one back.
The plus-one corrects for including the start.
Endpoint arithmetic prevents fence-post errors.
Share this: count tonight how many two-digit numbers divide by 7.

items.title: Factorial Zeros
items.question: Counting factors of 5, how many trailing zeros does twenty factorial end with?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Multiples of 5 up to 20 contribute four factors of 5, each pairing with a 2 to make one zero.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 4. Count factors of 5 in 20 factorial: 5, 10, 15, 20 give four, while factors of 2 are plentiful. Each 5 makes exactly one trailing zero.
items.lessonContent:
Trailing zeros count factor pairs of 2 and 5.
Fives are scarcer, so counting them decides the total.
Multiples of 25 contribute extra factors of 5.
Division chains tally contributions at every power.
Share this: predict tonight the trailing zeros of 30 factorial.

items.title: Doubled Remainder
items.question: A number divided by 7 leaves remainder 3. When that number is doubled, what remainder does the result leave when divided by 7?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Doubling the remainder 3 gives 6, which still fits below 7.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 6. Remainders scale with the number: double 3 to get 6, and since 6 is below the modulus no wrap-around occurs.
items.lessonContent:
Remainders transform alongside the numbers they track.
Scaling a remainder mirrors scaling the original.
Wrap around the modulus only when exceeding it.
Small cases verify the rule before trusting it.
Share this: predict tonight what tripling does to a remainder of 2 mod 7.

items.title: Thousand Split
items.question: The number 1001 factors into 7 times 11 times which remaining prime?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Dividing 1001 by 77 leaves 13, completing the famous triple factorization.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 13. Since 7 times 11 is 77 and 1001 divided by 77 is 13, the remaining prime factor is 13.
items.lessonContent:
Memorable factorizations unlock whole puzzle families.
Splitting off known factors exposes the hidden one.
Division verifies a claimed factorization instantly.
Famous numbers repay the memory invested in them.
Share this: factor 1001 aloud tonight from memory.

items.title: Repeated Block Factor
items.question: Every number formed by writing a three-digit block twice, such as 247247, is divisible by 1001. What is the smallest prime divisor of 1001?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Since 1001 equals 7 times 11 times 13, every repeated-block number inherits 7 as a divisor.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 7. Writing a block twice multiplies it by 1001, and 1001's prime factors begin with 7. Every such number is therefore a multiple of 7.
items.lessonContent:
Repeated blocks hide multiplication by repunit-like numbers.
Factoring the multiplier reveals guaranteed divisors.
Smallest prime factors give the sharpest universal claim.
Structure explains divisibility no trial division could see.
Share this: test tonight that your invented six-digit repeat divides by 7.
